clue.text: Music hall playing every hit — a treat!

indicators.note: playing with something means toying with it, so the letters are moved about freely

parts.note: the fodder, fourteen letters taken as written

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned music hall where every number on the bill is a crowd-pleaser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Music hall' reads as the setting of the scene, but it is the definition; everything after 'playing' is letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A music hall is the British name for a venue staging popular entertainment of mixed turns, songs and comic acts.

clue.text: A rating on a phone battery

indicators.note: on a telephone you only hear words, so what counts is how they would sound

parts.note: a rating is an ordinary sailor, and a salt is a seasoned sailor

explanation.surface: A star rating for how well a mobile phone battery performs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Phone battery' looks like one thing, but 'phone' belongs to the homophone signal and 'battery' is the legal term. Said quickly, 'a salt' is ASSAULT.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, battery is the actual use of force on another person, closely paired with assault and often used interchangeably.

clue.text: Graduate's silly to go round speaking like a native

indicators.note: going round something means circling it, so one word wraps around another

parts.note: idiotic means silly
a Master of Arts is a graduate

explanation.surface: A university graduate makes a fool of themselves trying to pass as a local while travelling.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining the two wordplay pieces into a sentence. MA is the usual crossword graduate.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatic language uses the natural expressions and turns of phrase that native speakers use, rather than textbook constructions.

clue.text: Bergamot is a neat ingredient for herbal tea

indicators.note: an ingredient is something contained within a mixture, so the answer sits inside the phrase

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and into the next three

explanation.surface: Bergamot, the citrus flavouring of Earl Grey, is a tidy addition to a herbal brew.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like kitchen advice about bergamot, but the answer lies in plain sight across the first four words.
explanation.definitionFit: A tisane is an infusion of dried leaves, flowers or herbs drunk in place of ordinary tea.

clue.text: Gathers hard work is in store for pupils

parts.note: tucks are gathers or folds sewn into fabric
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
op, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: Pupils face a tough school term ahead of them, with hard work in store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In store for' looks like an idiom meaning 'awaiting', but 'store for pupils' is the definition. OP (opus) is a standard crossword work.
explanation.definitionFit: A tuck shop is the small shop at a British school selling sweets and snacks to the children.

clue.text: Painter in Arles is fed drink periodically

indicators.note: to be fed is to have something put inside, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: est is French for 'is', as it would be said in the French town of Arles

indicators.note: something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: An artist in Arles, Van Gogh's town, kept supplied with drink at regular intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Arles' looks like a location for the painter, but it tells you to put 'is' into French. Max Ernst was a German Surrealist painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Max Ernst was a German-born artist, a leading figure of Dada and Surrealism, known for painting and collage.

clue.text: Soldier's uplifting story about love

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting something up makes it read from bottom to top
about means around, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: a report is a story in the news
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A soldier tells a heart-warming tale about falling in love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uplifting' reads as heart-warming, but in a down clue it turns the story upside down. The 's is 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A trooper is a private soldier, especially in a cavalry or armoured regiment.

clue.text: Doyens, say, among Bush's people

indicators.note: to be among others is to be in their midst, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: the elder is a bush, so its people are the elder's men
to state is to say

explanation.surface: Senior figures such as these were found in President Bush's administration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' suggests the American president, but here it is the elder shrub, and its people become 'elder's men' with STATE slotted in.
explanation.definitionFit: A doyen is the most respected senior member of a group, as elder statesmen are veteran figures whose experience earns deference.

clue.text: Rod getting caught by joint provides leverage

definitions.note: the answer is a noun for something that provides leverage

parts.note: a bar is a rod
gaining means getting
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: A rod jammed against a joint works as a lever, giving mechanical advantage.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about physical leverage; the answer is the negotiating sort. 'By' simply places the pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargaining chip is something held in reserve to trade in negotiation, giving its holder power to extract concessions.

clue.text: Before cruises, outspoken sailor lets himself down

indicators.note: one thing coming before another puts it first in the sequence

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

indicators.note: outspoken words are said out loud, so their sound matters

parts.note: to cruise is to sail

explanation.surface: A blunt-talking sailor disgraces himself before going on cruises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lets himself down' suggests disgrace, but it means descending a rope. The second half of the answer is said like 'sails' though spelt the German way.
explanation.definitionFit: To abseil is to descend a rock face or wall on a rope, controlling the drop oneself.

clue.text: Vote against either side in Carlsbad agreement

parts.note: a con is a vote against, as in pros and cons

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another
the sides of a word are its two ends, so only its outer letters are kept

parts.note: its first and last letters
'either' pairs with 'or'

explanation.surface: Someone in Carlsbad votes against both sides of a proposed deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Either side' looks like one phrase meaning both parties, but it splits: 'either' supplies OR, and 'side' picks the ends of the town's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Concord is harmony or accord between people or nations, and also a formal treaty settling a dispute.

clue.text: Food lovers try with rums and nuts

parts.note: to have a go is to try

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, and crazy letters fall out of their proper order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Gourmets sample a dessert flavoured with rum and nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rums and nuts' sounds like ingredients, but 'nuts' is the signal to rearrange the seven letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A gourmand is a person who enjoys eating heartily, sometimes greedily, and takes great pleasure in good dishes.

clue.text: Lush plant in fresh soil from the east

indicators.note: in an across entry, reading from the east means right to left, backwards

parts.note: to repot a plant is to put it in fresh soil

explanation.surface: A lush, green plant thrives when given fresh soil from the east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lush' looks like an adjective for thriving greenery, but it is the noun for a heavy drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Lush is slang for a habitual drunkard, and a toper is an old word for someone who drinks to excess.

clue.text: Thoroughly trendy dog found in Oz

parts.note: what is in is fashionable
Toto is Dorothy's dog in The Wizard of Oz

explanation.surface: A thoroughly fashionable dog turns up in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oz' suggests Australia, a common slang name, but here it is the land of The Wizard of Oz.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means as a whole or entirely, so it serves as an adverb for completely or thoroughly.

clue.text: Boat's front bit attached to its prow at sea

definitions.text: Boat's front bit attached to its prow at sea

indicators.note: attaching joins one piece directly onto the next
the front of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter

indicators.note: at sea means confused and adrift, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A description of a spar fixed to a ship's bow out on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: read straight it describes the spar projecting from the bow; read cryptically it gives a first letter plus a jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowsprit is the spar running forward from a sailing ship's stem, to which the forestays are fastened.

clue.text: Desire, perhaps represented by Sartre, etc

indicators.note: to represent is to present again in a new form, so the letters take another shape

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Desire as a theme explored by Sartre and other existentialist philosophers.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennessee Williams's play is A Streetcar Named Desire, so Desire is an example of a tram by name; 'perhaps' flags that.
explanation.definitionFit: In the famous Williams play, Desire is the name of a New Orleans tram line, so it is one instance.

clue.text: Married in Croatia, plastered with perfume

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another
plastered means very drunk, and drunk letters stagger out of order

parts.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for married

explanation.surface: A newly-wed in Croatia gets drunk and is doused in scent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastered' reads as both drunk and smeared, fitting the perfume, but it only signals the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: Something aromatic has a strong pleasant smell, as anything scented with perfume does.

clue.text: Afraid of current, next to river keeping dry

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another
next to puts one piece immediately beside another

parts.note: what is current is in fashion
the Ure is a Yorkshire river
sec is the wine term for dry

explanation.surface: Someone afraid of the river's current stays on the bank to keep dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like flowing water beside the river, but it means fashionable. The Ure is a river in Yorkshire, northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: To feel insecure is to lack confidence and be anxious or fearful about something.

clue.text: Big name placed over new business

parts.note: a star is a big name

indicators.note: over can mean turned over, so the word is flipped to read backwards

parts.note: put means placed

explanation.surface: A celebrity is put in charge of a newly launched company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Placed over' reads as put in charge of, but 'over' turns the word for placed upside down in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A start-up is a newly established company, typically a small one in its early stages of growth.

clue.text: Good health argument supporting rest

indicators.note: a supporter stands behind or alongside, so one piece is joined to the other

parts.note: a pro is an argument in favour
to sit is to rest

explanation.surface: A health argument in favour of getting more rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good health' is a toast here, not wellbeing; PROSIT is the German and Latin drinking toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Prosit is a toast said when raising glasses, wishing those drinking well, just as 'good health' is.

clue.text: Worker in a novel initially, not still here?

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: She is a novel by H. Rider Haggard
the worker bee

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only a first letter is kept

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: A worker in a novel is apparently no longer present at the scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not still here' reads as 'gone', but 'not' only gives its initial, leaving 'still here?' as a playful definition: an illicit still might supply the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A shebeen is an unlicensed Irish or Scottish drinking den, where moonshine from a hidden still would be served.

clue.text: Textbook three, maybe third of three

parts.note: three is an example of a prime number

indicators.note: the third of a word means its third letter alone

parts.note: the letter in third place

explanation.surface: Volume three of a textbook series, or perhaps the third of three volumes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks three as an example of a prime, not a definition of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A primer is an elementary schoolbook introducing the basics of a subject, such as reading.

clue.text: Acute accent

definitions.meaning: first meaning: serious, severe, as in an acute crisis
second meaning: the backward-sloping mark over a vowel

explanation.walkthrough: 'Acute accent' is a real mark, the opposite of the answer's mark; split the words and acute means serious.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means serious or critical, and the noun names the diacritic sloping down left to right, as in French è.

clue.text: Wear what the chap did on 'is 'orse

indicators.note: the missing aitches mimic a Cockney accent, which drops every initial H, so that letter goes

parts.note: the chap is he
what one did on a horse was ride, in the past tense

explanation.surface: A Cockney describes what the bloke did on his horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney, the London working-class accent, drops initial H sounds, as the clue's own apostrophes show, so the chap loses his H too.
explanation.definitionFit: To wear something down is to erode it, gradually rubbing or washing material away.

clue.text: Killer before entering beat back bodyguards

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it
going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: to drum is to beat
ere is an old word for before
the SS was Hitler's bodyguard unit

explanation.surface: A killer, before entering, beats back a group of bodyguards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' looks like a time word in the story, but it is a piece itself. The SS began as the Nazi leader's personal guard.
explanation.definitionFit: A murderess is a woman who kills another person unlawfully, the dated feminine form of murderer.

clue.text: Keen to pay without delay

parts.note: hot on something means keen on it
to foot the bill is to pay

explanation.surface: Someone eager to settle a bill promptly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one idea, eagerness to pay promptly, but splits into three parts with the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotfoot is an adverb meaning hastily or in eager haste, as in rushing somewhere at once.

clue.text: Staff guarding the new chopper

indicators.note: a guard surrounds what it protects, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: a mace is a ceremonial staff

indicators.note: something new is made afresh, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Staff are protecting the new helicopter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like employees and 'chopper' like a helicopter; they are a ceremonial rod and a cutting blade.
explanation.definitionFit: A machete is a broad heavy knife used for chopping through vegetation or cane.

clue.text: Regular fee one ground typically slashed

parts.note: a peppercorn is something usually ground before use
rent means torn or slashed

explanation.surface: A standard fee that has typically been slashed to one figure.
explanation.walkthrough: A peppercorn rent is a nominal sum, a British legal term from the custom of charging a single peppercorn a year.
explanation.definitionFit: Rent is a fee paid at regular intervals; a peppercorn rent is merely a token amount kept to preserve a lease.
